why: The set law of the framework-owned interaction selection, written once and read by two implementations: the Rust reducer laws (`🧪️tests/🔬️plugin-runtime-plugin-builder-contract/🦀️.rs`, driving the real reserved `interactionSelect` job) and the language-neutral Node twin (`interactionSelectionSetOracle`, the renderer react target's `📜️script.ts`). A selection is a SET of topology ids: `Select` is event-sourced, so it must be idempotent per id — repeating a target in one batch, or re-adding an already selected id, can never make the same id appear twice in the published `selectedIds`.
liveDefect: Ticket 26/09/09/PROCEDURAL-3D-END-TO-END, 2026-09-12: one click on the generation3d preview published `InteractionView {"selectedIds":["extrude@solid","extrude@solid"],"publishedIds":["extrude@solid","extrude@solid"],"locked":{"extrude@solid":false}}`. The per-domain reducer was innocent (`next_selection` already dedups `Replace`/`Additive`); the leftover PROJECTION flattened every domain of one `InteractionState`, and the framework deliberately mirrors the picked ids into a second `vortex` domain (`overlay_leftover_ids_into_vortex`), so one pick was counted once per mirroring domain. `locked` — an object, keyed by construction — carried the id exactly once, which is what made the two halves disagree.
law: selectedIds names every selected topology id AT MOST ONCE, in first-seen order, for every merge and however many mirror domains the leftover projection flattens; `locked` has exactly one key per published id, and `gumball.anchorId` is the first of them.

cases.why: Two rendered instances of ONE topology id picked in one batch select that id once — the host is expected to collapse them first, and the reducer must not depend on it having done so.
The regression itself: a plain one-target pick must publish ONE id even though the leftover state carries the picked id under both the app's domain and the `vortex` mirror.
Event-sourced `Select`: re-adding a selected id is a no-op, never a second entry.
An additive merge still grows the set — the dedup must not swallow a genuinely new id.
A repeated target inside an additive batch lands once.

wiring.why: Source-level anchors the Node twin re-checks, so the two flatten sites can never drift back apart into one deduping and one not — which is exactly how the live defect was introduced.
wiring.lockedFromSelectedIds: let locked: Vec<(String, DslValue)> = selected_ids.iter().map(|id| (id.clone(), DslValue::Bool(false))).collect();
